questions.q: What is the purpose of a fermion-to-qubit mapping (like Jordan-Wigner) in molecular VQE?
options: It converts the electronic Hamiltonian's fermionic operators into a weighted sum of Pauli strings that a quantum circuit can measure
It converts a classical computer program into a quantum circuit automatically
It eliminates the need for a basis set when describing molecular orbitals
It replaces the variational principle with an exact diagonalization method
questions.explain: Jordan-Wigner (and alternatives like Bravyi-Kitaev) rewrite the fermionic electronic Hamiltonian as a weighted sum of Pauli strings -- operators like Z_0 or X_0X_1 -- which is exactly the form a VQE circuit measures term by term.

questions.q: Why is H2 (the hydrogen molecule) the standard 'hello world' benchmark for molecular VQE?
options: In a minimal STO-3G basis its Hamiltonian maps to just 2-4 qubits, small enough to run on today's hardware while still being a genuine quantum chemistry problem
Because H2 is the largest molecule that has ever been simulated with any quantum algorithm
Because H2 has no known classical solution to compare against
Because H2's ground state energy is exactly 0 Hartree, making comparison trivial
questions.explain: H2 in a minimal basis is small enough (2-4 qubits) to actually run on noisy current hardware while remaining a real quantum chemistry problem, which is why it is used across essentially all VQE tutorials and papers as a benchmark.

questions.q: What does 'chemical accuracy' mean, and why does the lesson emphasize it as a demanding bar?
options: Agreement with the true energy to within about 1.6 milli-Hartree (~1 kcal/mol) -- a much tighter standard than being merely 'close' in a loose sense, and the scale that determines whether a predicted reaction is favorable
Any VQE result within 1 full Hartree of the correct answer
A measure of how many qubits a VQE circuit uses
The accuracy of the classical optimizer's convergence criterion only, unrelated to the energy value itself
questions.explain: Chemical accuracy (~1.6 milli-Hartree) is a much stricter bar than loose closeness, and the lesson is explicit that a result 'close' within 0.1 Hartree is not chemically useful -- reaching and sustaining true chemical accuracy under real hardware noise is a substantially harder target.

questions.q: According to the lesson's honest accounting, what has VQE actually demonstrated so far, and what has it NOT demonstrated?
options: It has reproduced known ground-state energies for small molecules (H2, LiH, BeH2) as a proof of concept, but has not outperformed classical methods like coupled-cluster theory or DFT on any molecule of practical scientific or industrial interest
It has already outperformed all classical quantum chemistry methods on industrially relevant molecules
It has demonstrated nothing at all, even on the smallest toy molecules
It has replaced classical chemistry methods entirely for molecules of any size
questions.explain: The lesson states plainly that VQE is validated as a proof of concept on small molecules but has not yet outperformed classical quantum chemistry methods on any molecule large enough to matter scientifically or industrially -- consistent with the course's honest-benchmarking theme.

questions.q: What role does the commonly cited H2 benchmark value of approximately -1.137 Hartree play in this lesson?
options: It serves as the known reference answer that a VQE implementation's result is checked against, the same role the exact eigenvalue played for the toy Hamiltonian in Lesson 11
It is a value this course derived from scratch via its own simulation
It represents the energy of a molecule with no electrons at all
It is the exact chemical-accuracy threshold itself, not an energy value
questions.explain: The lesson presents -1.137 Hartree as a widely reproduced literature reference value (not something derived in this course) used to check whether a VQE run reached the right answer -- paralleling how Lesson 11 used an exactly computed eigenvalue as its own ground-truth check.
